title: What not to put on the site for a consumer brand
metaTitle: What to cut from a consumer brand site
excerpt: Cut the manifesto that sits in front of the product. Keep the object, shown clearly, and a direct way to see it. A shorter site that tells the truth is the shop.
alt: A white geometric building with a glass wing and a cantilevered upper volume. A structure reduced to its necessary forms, which is the edit a brand site needs.

faqs.question: What should come off a brand homepage first?
faqs.answer: The manifesto that arrives before the object, including the film, the landscape, and the values row that never names the goods. One true sentence can sit under the product. The longer creed can live on the about page for someone who opts into it.

faqs.question: Which pages are enough?
faqs.answer: Home, catalog, product, a short about page with a real person, contact with a true reply time, and the policies you are obliged to publish. Add repair when it has its own rules. Refuse a page whose only job is to make the brand seem larger.

faqs.question: How do you test the cut?
faqs.answer: Read the homepage as if the speech were deleted. If the object, the path, and the price shape still make sense, you have a shop. If the page collapses without the creed, the creed was holding up the wrong thing.

markdown:
Consumer brand website mistakes often begin with a manifesto that sits in front of the product. It reassures the team and confuses a shopper who does not know you yet. Keep the object, shown clearly, and a clear way to see the product. A shorter site that tells the truth will do more than a long site that performs taste.

The cut is editorial. Every block you remove makes the object easier to find, and easier to believe.

## The manifesto, in all its costumes

The obvious version is a full-screen creed about how the world should feel, with the product somewhere below. The quieter versions do the same job. A cinematic video with no object. A landscape that stands in for the goods. A row of abstract values. A founder's letter about awakening. A campaign line that could belong to any careful brand. Each one is the company talking to itself.

Move belief to a place that has earned it. One sentence under the product, about material or method, if that fact changes the purchase. A longer account on the about page, for the shopper who already cares. A proof page for a single decision, linked from the object it changed. The homepage is the counter. The counter shows the goods.

Google's guide to [helpful, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether the page has a real audience who would find it useful if they came directly, and whether they leave able to do the thing they came to do. It also says not to write to a word count you heard a search engine wanted. A brand site padded with essays, so that it looks deep, fails both. The audience came to see the product. Depth is a clear object, an honest price, and a person behind the work.

Apply the same test to a journal that never touches the goods. If the essays do not help someone choose, understand care, or see a decision you made, the journal is a manifesto with a publishing schedule. Stop the schedule, or aim every piece at a product fact.

## Pages and blocks that can leave

A playlist, a city guide, a collage of press pulled ahead of the catalog, a loyalty club with no real benefit: these flatter the team and delay the shopper. Press can sit small, low, and true. A city guide can be a personal project somewhere else. The shop has a job.

Stale campaigns are a cut. Last season's line, still in the header, tells a new shopper you are not watching the store. Remove it when the season ends. If the product remains, fold it into the ordinary catalog with ordinary pictures. A campaign that has become the permanent homepage is how a temporary mood replaces the range.

Duplicate claims should go. If the material is explained on the product page, the homepage should not paraphrase it in vaguer words. Two descriptions drift. One source, linked. The same rule covers shipping, lead times, and returns. A banner that contradicts the product page is a manifesto of urgency, and it trains people to distrust the number.

Stock photographs of lives you do not sell are a cut even when the lighting is beautiful. They are taste performing as content. The shopper cannot buy the stock scene. Wabisabi, a public Hanabi brand site, is a reminder that calm can be made of real objects. Down the Cove, the public ecommerce redesign and migration, is a reminder that a shop can be rebuilt without burying the catalog under a speech. Use them as standards for what to keep in frame.

## What stays, in order

Keep a homepage that shows the object and a way to see the product. Keep the menu in shop language. Keep prices with the shape visible: the number, the unit, what is included, what is not, how long it takes if it is made to order. Keep photographs that name the thing. Keep a short about page with a real person and a real method. Keep a contact path with a true reply time. Keep shipping and returns in one findable sentence.

That set is a complete site for a shopper who does not know you. It can be a small number of templates: home, catalog, product, about, contact, policy. Add a page when an offer has its own rules, such as repair. Refuse a page whose only job is to make the brand seem larger.

Policies you are obliged to publish stay. They stay as themselves, linked and dated. Privacy, returns, and any product-safety note. Leading with them is unnecessary. Hiding them is how a careful visual brand becomes careless in the one place a dispute will look. The lead remains the object.

A size guide, a care note, and a materials line stay attached to the product they describe. They are part of seeing the product. They are not separate campaigns. Write them in the same voice as the price. Short sentences. Concrete nouns. A care note that turns into a poem will not be followed, and the object will be damaged, and the brand will be blamed.

## Taste is a weak reason to add a block

Blocks survive because they look like brands the team admires. A giant quote. A horizontal scroll of textures. An animated counter of "pieces made." Admiration is not a job. Ask what the shopper can do after the block that they could not do before. If the answer is only that they will feel something, check whether a clear picture of the object already did that.

Counters are a temptation because they imitate evidence. A spinning number of community members rarely helps someone choose a mug. If you have a true, useful fact, write a sentence. "The sole can be replaced, and we still stock it." That sentence is evidence. A counter is a costume.

Music, custom cursors, and long intros delay the product. On a phone in a public place they can be embarrassing, which is a poor introduction to an object you hope someone will live with. Let the page be still unless motion reveals a product fact, such as a detail opening. Honor reduced motion with a still page that carries the same information.

The [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) are a brake on taste. Content should be perceivable and operable. A menu that only appears on hover, a price baked into a photograph, a video with no path to the product: these choices remove the shop from some of the people you want. Cut them in favor of text, buttons, and a picture with a real text alternative.

## A shorter site stays true

Every extra page can go stale. A short site has a chance of matching the workshop in November. Assign an owner to home, catalog, product facts, about, and the inbox. If a page has no owner, it is a candidate to cut. Review on a phone at the start of a season. Can a stranger name the object. Is the price current. Does any creed sit above the goods. Fix those. Ignore the neighboring brand's new microsite.

Hanabi's work in this mood is the same habit. Decide what the first screen must prove, then remove what argues with it. The studio designs and builds. The brand still has to know which object leads, and which sentence is true. A page cannot supply either.

When the remaining pages agree, keep them agreed. The homepage shows the object. The product page shows the price shape. The about page shows a person. The contact page makes a promise you keep. If one drifts back into a speech, pull it back. The set is the shop.

Look at the footer with the same suspicion. Newsletter popups, a row of social icons that open abandoned accounts, and a chat bubble that nobody staffs are small manifestos. They say the brand is busy. They cover the product. Keep a quiet link to the one channel you actually answer.

Then read the homepage with the manifesto deleted in your head. If the object, the path, and the price shape still make sense, you have a shop. If the page collapses without the speech, the speech was load-bearing in the wrong place. Move one true sentence under the product and let the rest of the creed live where a curious person can opt into it.


If the creed still feels essential, put it on the about page under a heading a curious person can choose. The homepage has already spent its first view.

## The next buyer has two sides

A consumer brand loses shoppers by speaking before it shows the goods. A two-sided marketplace has a different first proof, because the visitor may be either side, and the homepage has to show which door is which. The piece that takes up that problem is [what the homepage has to prove for a two-sided marketplace](/blog/what-the-homepage-has-to-prove-for-a-two-sided-marketplace).

If you are about to rebuild and you want a second opinion on what to cut, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the current homepage and say which object you would hand a stranger first.
